mainEntity.name: How accurate is the U.S. Navy body fat method?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is a field estimate and measurement error can be meaningful. Accuracy varies with body composition, measurement technique and the method used; it should not be treated as equivalent to a clinical body-composition measurement.

mainEntity.name: Why does the formula differ for men and women?

acceptedAnswer.text: Body fat distribution patterns differ by sex, so the formula includes hip measurement for women to account for typical fat distribution differences.

mainEntity.name: What is a healthy body fat percentage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reference ranges for body fat vary by age, sex, population and source. These categories are educational reference points, not personalized medical targets or diagnoses.

mainEntity.name: How often should I re-measure my body fat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Monthly is a reasonable cadence for tracking meaningful change — body fat percentage doesn't shift dramatically week to week, so frequent measurement mostly captures measurement noise rather than real change.

mainEntity.name: How does the Navy method compare to a DEXA scan?

acceptedAnswer.text: DEXA and circumference methods use different measurement approaches. A DEXA result should not be treated as a simple conversion or guaranteed ground truth for an individual; the Navy result is best used as a consistent field estimate.

mainEntity.name: Where exactly should I measure my waist and neck?

acceptedAnswer.text: Waist is typically measured at the navel level, and neck just below the larynx — consistent placement each time you measure matters more than the exact spot, for tracking change over time.

mainEntity.name: Tape measure or skinfold calipers — which is better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both are estimates. Skinfolds taken by a trained person can be quite accurate, but results vary a lot with technique; the tape method is easier to repeat consistently at home. Pick one and use it the same way each time.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate fat mass and lean mass from body fat percentage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fat mass is your weight multiplied by your body fat percentage, and lean mass is what remains. At 80 kg and 25%, fat mass is 20 kg and lean mass is 60 kg.

mainEntity.name: What would I weigh at a lower body fat percentage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide your lean mass by (1 minus the target percentage). With 60 kg of lean mass, 20% body fat is 60 ÷ 0.80 = 75 kg. This assumes lean mass stays the same, which is rarely exactly true, so use it as a rough guide.

mainEntity.name: Is body fat percentage better than BMI?

acceptedAnswer.text: They answer different questions. BMI only uses height and weight, so it cannot tell muscle from fat. Body fat percentage separates fat from lean mass, but its estimates have their own error, so many people track both.

mainEntity.name: Why do the Navy and skinfold methods give different results?

acceptedAnswer.text: They measure different things: the Navy method infers fat from circumferences and height, while skinfolds estimate body density from fat folds under the skin. Each has its own error, so compare results from the same method over time.

mainEntity.name: Is the Navy method reliable for very muscular people?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is less reliable. Waist and neck circumferences reflect muscle as well as fat, so the formula can misjudge people whose build differs from the population it was based on. Use it for tracking trends rather than as an exact figure.
